newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE - Fears of Peronist backlash against Argentina's reforms.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Fears of Peronist backlash against Argentina's reforms.

text.p: "Why are Peronists like camels?" goes a joke currently doing the rounds in Argentina, where Peronist President Carlos Menem, and everyone else of Middle Eastern ancestry, is known as El Turco -- The Turk.
"Because even when they're dying of hunger and thirst, they still follow the Turk."

But the camels' loyalty is being severely tested and soothsayers predict El Turco's caravan may well be smaller by the mid-term Congressional elections in October, when half the seats in the Chamber of Deputies will be up for grabs.

With Menem's popularity at its lowest since he came to power in 1989, unemployment refusing to budge from record highs and trade unions, businesses and the government at loggerheads over how to create jobs, the outlook is unsteady for the Peronists' absolute majority in the lower house.

While analysts rule out the Peronists being pushed into second place and point out that the party is so lacking in discipline that Menem rarely has its full support anyway, they fear for the pace of economic and institutional reforms if the result is poor.
PRESSURE TO PERONIZE ECONOMY

"If they lose by a big percentage there could be pressure to "Peronize" the economy ahead of the presidential elections in 1999," said the chief economist of a major Argentine bank, using the common terminology for the feared blacklash from old-guard Peronists against Menem's free-market reforms.
Menem is not allowed to stand for a third consecutive term in 1999, but the outcome of this election could define the reformist profile and platform of his successor.

The big issue is clear: Menem's failure to combine his success on inflation and privatisation with job creation. Unemployment is now 17.3 percent, compared with 6.9 percent at the 1991 launch of the Convertibility Plan for stability.

Early 1997 opinion polls make depressing reading for Menem. The latest, by Carlos Azzariti, clearly shows the main public concern at 38 percent is unemployment, followed by 14 percent who want Menem out. Corruption and the slow pace of justice, both long-standing Peronist weaknesses, follow close behind.
A poll by Graciela Romer shows a 79 percent disapproval rating for Menem, with 60 percent blaming his policies for Argentina's high unemployment.
GLOOM ON JOBS FRONT

Deep public and corporate pessimism contradict official forecasts of a 2-4 percentage point drop in unemployment this year. A Gallup poll shows 45 percent of the public expects it to rise and 51 percent are braced for a year of conflicts and strikes. An Argentine Industrial Union (UIA) business lobby poll shows 60 percent of big firms share that view on jobs.
In this gloomy context, there is an air of resignation in party ranks.
"If the elections were today, there's no doubt we would have serious difficulties," says Peronist deputy and former economy and defence minister Antonio Erman Gonzalez.

"If the executive does not take the right steps to bring transparency and ethics to its administration, Peronism might not only lose this Congressional election but could also lose the chance to keep hold of power in 1999," warned Senator Antonio Cafiero, a minister under General Juan Peron back in the 1950s.

Menem, who tells his anti-reform critics that his brand of Peronism is merely an "aggornamento" of the general's, is now at a decisive stage in the longest-delayed of his reforms -- an overhaul of labour legislation dating from Peron's rule.
LABOUR REFORMS KEY TO GROWTH

"Labour reforms have been on the menu since 1989 and if they are the last reforms to be tackled, it's because they are the toughest," says ING Barings economist Freddy Thomsen, who thinks reform will inevitably slow down as the year wears on.

The government admits it needs to find 400,000 jobs lost in the so-called Tequila recession when the backlash from Mexican devaluation in 1994 sent Argentine bank deposits running for shelter and caused a 4.4 percent shrinkage of the economy the following year.

Social Security Secretary Carlos Torres is counting on the 5-6 percent economic growth expected this year for 150,000. More jobs will be created only if employers are liberated from high labour costs, the government says.
"Argentina's economic expansion will eventually hit a wall without payroll tax cuts and labour deregulation," said Mike Churchill, an analyst in Washington for Polyconomics.

After the main CGT labour federation led its third general strike on December 26 last year, Menem lost his patience and signed three decrees reducing union control of collective pay bargaining. Other reforms, such as replacing redundancy payouts with unemployment insurance, are more palatable to the unions and were to be thrashed out in Congress.
But Argentine labour courts threw out the decrees as unconstitutional, and Menem's ministers had to ask the CGT to return to the negotiating table.
BUSINESS UNDER FIRE TO CREATE JOBS

Cocksure after the court rulings and after Menem ticked off employers at a party summit for "not being active enough in creating jobs," CGT chief Rodolfo Daer says he will take a whole "list of demands" into fresh three-way talks with the government and business leaders on employment policy.

Business leaders, mindful perhaps of the Peronist "social pact" in 1973 which brought huge pay rises and price controls, are smarting at what UIA chief Jorge Blanco Villegas called a "worrying government about-face" and have changed their demand for labour reform by consensus to calls for tough decrees.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Raul Buonnuome believes Menem is merely forcing Argentine firms to take responsibility for labour reforms, while unions are trying to delay the inevitable loss of control over pay talks and healthcare.

"It's a matter of timing, and perhaps the labour reform is going to be less profound, but clearly it is going to happen," he says. "Anyway, you cannot hope to change in two years labour legislation that has been in place for 40 or 50."

But neither should fans of rapid reform read too much into Menem's talk of Domingo Cavallo, the former economy minister who was behind his economic successes but was sacked last July, being allowed to run on a Peronist ticket in October.
Analysts believe it is a classic Menem ruse to scupper any plans of Peronist dissidents to regroup around Cavallo, under an anti-corruption flag, and steal votes from the party.
